odin.summary: Highest of the Æsir, half giant on his mother's side, and already promised to the wolf.
odin.description: Óðinn is the eldest and highest of the Æsir, and the least safe of them. Snorri traces his descent through Borr to Bestla, daughter of the giant Bǫlþorn — which makes the chief of the gods half a giant, and puts him on both sides of the war he will lose. He is a god of wisdom bought at a price: an eye at Mímir's well, nine nights on the windy tree. He rides to Ragnarǫk first, in a gold helmet, carrying the spear Gungnir, and is swallowed by Fenrir, the son of his own blood-brother.

thor.summary: Strongest of the gods, son of Óðinn and Earth, and the serpent's opposite number.
thor.description: Þórr is the strongest of gods and men, son of Óðinn by Jǫrð, the Earth. He holds Þrúðvangar and the hall Bilskirnir, and owns three things of great price, of which the hammer Mjǫllnir is the first. His life is a long argument with giants, and it ends in the middle of one: at Ragnarǫk he kills Jǫrmungandr, walks nine paces away from the body, and falls dead of its venom. The serpent is Loki's son. So is the wolf that takes his father.

frigg.epithet: Wife of Óðinn, mother of Baldr
frigg.summary: She knows every fate and prophesies none of them.
frigg.description: Frigg, daughter of Fjǫrgynn, is Óðinn's wife and the foremost of the goddesses. Snorri says she knows all the fates of men though she speaks no prophecy, which is a bleak thing to know about someone. When her son Baldr dreams of his death she takes an oath from every thing in the world to spare him, and misses one shoot of mistletoe because she thought it too young to ask. Loki asks her the right question in the shape of a woman, and she answers it.

baldr.summary: Best of the Æsir, killed by his blind brother, and one of the few who come back.
baldr.description: Baldr is the second son of Óðinn, so fair that light comes off him, and so gracious that none may gainsay his judgments. His death is the hinge of the whole cycle: the gods lose him to a shoot of mistletoe, the one thing his mother did not think to ask, thrown by his blind brother Hǫðr with Loki standing behind him aiming. He goes to Hel and does not come back — until after Ragnarǫk, when he and Hǫðr return together to a world that has burnt.

hod.summary: He throws the shot that kills his brother, and does not see it.
hod.description: Hǫðr is blind, and strong enough. Snorri says the gods would rather not have to name him, because the work of his hands will be remembered a long time. He stands outside the ring at the game where the Æsir throw things at Baldr for the pleasure of watching them not land, and Loki asks him why he is not joining in, and offers to aim for him. Skaldic convention calls him the Blind God, Baldr's Slayer, Thrower of the Mistletoe, and Son of Óðinn — four names for one afternoon. He returns from Hel with Baldr afterwards.

tyr.summary: He fed the wolf, and paid for the binding with his sword hand.
tyr.description: Týr is the boldest of the Æsir, a god of victory and of the courage to stand still. When the gods raised Fenrir in Ásgarðr he was the only one who dared bring the wolf its meat. When they came to bind it with Gleipnir the wolf demanded a pledge, and Týr put his hand into its mouth knowing what the pledge meant. Skaldic verse calls him the One-handed God and, in the same breath, Fosterer of the Wolf. At Ragnarǫk he and the hound Garmr kill each other.

heimdall.summary: He hears grass grow, blows the horn that starts the end, and dies fighting Loki.
heimdall.description: Heimdallr is the White God, born of nine sisters, who keeps watch at Himinbjǫrg where Bifrǫst meets heaven. He needs less sleep than a bird, sees a hundred leagues by night or day, and hears wool growing on a sheep. Whether Óðinn fathered him is not settled: Snorri gives him nine mothers in one chapter and calls him Óðinn's son in another. He blows Gjallarhorn to wake the gods for the last battle, and there he and Loki kill each other — the watchman and the one thing he was watching for.

vidar.summary: He says nothing, and he is the one who avenges Óðinn.
vidar.description: Víðarr is called the silent god, nearly as strong as Þórr, and the gods trust him in every struggle. He has a thick shoe made of every scrap of leather ever trimmed from a toe or a heel, saved up across all time for one step. When Fenrir has swallowed his father he puts that foot on the wolf's lower jaw and takes the upper in his hand. How he finishes it depends on who is telling: Snorri has him tear the jaws apart, Vǫluspá has him drive a sword to the heart. He walks out of Ragnarǫk alive.

sif.summary: Her hair was cut off by Loki, and replaced with gold made by dwarves.
sif.description: Sif is Þórr's wife and the mother of Ullr, who is Þórr's stepson. Loki cut off all her hair for mischief and, on being caught, promised the Black Elves would make her more; the dwarves who did it made Skíðblaðnir and the spear Gungnir in the same sitting, which is how the gods came by most of their treasures. She has fewer relations recorded here than she should, and that gap is itemized in the project's data notes rather than papered over.

njord.summary: A Van living among the Æsir as a hostage, father of Freyr and Freyja.
njord.description: Njǫrðr rules the course of the wind and stills sea and fire, and men call on him for voyages and for hunting. He is not of the race of the Æsir at all: he was raised among the Vanir and handed over as a hostage when the two families of gods made peace, with Hœnir going the other way. At Nóatún he fathered Freyr and Freyja, which means the Vanir line inside Ásgarðr runs entirely through a prisoner of war.

freyr.summary: He gave away his sword for a giantess, and at Ragnarǫk he needs it.
freyr.description: Freyr governs rain and sunshine and the fruit of the earth, and is the most renowned of the gods after the Æsir proper. He gave his good sword to his messenger Skírnir to win the giantess Gerðr. Snorri is blunt about the cost: at Ragnarǫk he faces Surtr, and the fight is hard, and he falls, and the reason he falls is that he no longer has that sword. It is the clearest case in the cycle of an ending being set up centuries in advance by an ordinary decision.

freyja.summary: Njǫrðr's daughter, Freyr's sister, and she takes half the slain.
freyja.description: Freyja is the most renowned of the goddesses. She has the hall Fólkvangr, and wherever she rides to battle she takes half the killed and Óðinn the other half — a division that puts a Vanir hostage's daughter on equal terms with the All-father. She is Njǫrðr's daughter and Freyr's sister, wife of Óðr, owner of the necklace Brísingamen, which Loki once stole and Heimdallr once fought him for.

loki.summary: Counted among the Æsir, fathered by a giant, and the parent of everything that ends them.
loki.description: Loki is the pivot of the whole graph. Snorri numbers him among the Æsir and calls him the mischief-monger of the Æsir in the same sentence, then names his father Fárbauti the giant. He and Óðinn mixed blood in olden days, which Loki reminds him of when he wants a drink. With the giantess Angrboða he fathers Fenrir, Jǫrmungandr and Hel. He brings about Baldr's death, and is bound for it. At Ragnarǫk he steers the ship of the dead, and he and Heimdallr kill each other. Isolate his descendants and you have recovered most of the opposing side.

surtr.summary: He has stood at the border of the fire-world since before the world was shaped, waiting.
surtr.description: Surtr sits at the land's end of Múspell to defend it, and has done since before the earth was made — the fire-world is the first world to exist, older than the gods who will burn in it. His sword throws off more light than the sun. When the end comes he rides out first, with fire before him and behind him, and Bifrǫst breaks under the riders. He kills Freyr, and then flings fire over the earth and burns the whole world. He is the only figure here who was in position from the beginning.

angrboda.summary: Mother of the wolf, the serpent and Hel.
angrboda.description: Angrboða is a giantess in Jǫtunheimr, and she is in the sources for exactly one reason: with Loki she has three children, and those three are Fenrir, Jǫrmungandr and Hel. When the gods learned that this kindred was being raised in Jǫtunheimr, and prophecy told them what it meant, they took the children — and every step they took to contain them is a step towards the ending they were trying to avoid.

farbauti.summary: Loki's father, named twice and never described.
farbauti.description: Fárbauti is named as Loki's father in Gylfaginning and again in the kenning lists, and that is all the corpus gives. The name has been read as something like cruel-striker, but the texts do not gloss it. He matters structurally rather than narratively: he is the reason Loki is a giant's son sitting inside Ásgarðr, and the reason Loki's children are a giant's grandchildren.

laufey.summary: Loki's mother, and the parent he is named for.
laufey.description: Laufey, also called Nál, is Loki's mother. Snorri names her alongside Fárbauti and moves on. What is unusual is that Loki is repeatedly called Laufeyjarson, son of Laufey, rather than by his father's name — the reverse of the normal patronymic — and the sources never explain it. Whether she is a giantess or of some other kind is not stated; this project classes her with the jǫtnar and flags the classification as contested.

bestla.summary: A giant's daughter, and the mother of Óðinn.
bestla.description: Bestla is the daughter of the giant Bǫlþorn, and Borr took her to wife; their sons were Óðinn, Vili and Vé. She is a single sentence in the sources, and that sentence rearranges everything downstream of it — the gods who spend the whole cycle fighting giants are themselves half giant, through her, and Óðinn's most important teacher may have been her brother.

bolthorn.summary: Óðinn's grandfather, from whose son Óðinn learned nine songs.
bolthorn.description: Bǫlþorn is a giant, Bestla's father, and therefore Óðinn's maternal grandfather. He appears twice: once in Snorri's genealogy, and once in Hávamál, where Óðinn says he took nine mighty songs from the son of Bǫlþorn — his own uncle, unnamed. The wisdom that makes Óðinn Óðinn comes to him from the giants' side of the family.

ymir.summary: Born from melting rime before the earth existed, and killed by his own great-grandsons to make it.
ymir.description: Ymir forms when warm air off Múspell meets the rime of Niflheim in the Yawning Void, before there is an earth to stand on. He sweats a son and a daughter from under his arm, and one of his legs fathers a son on the other — the whole race of Rime-Giants descends from him without a mother anywhere in it. Auðumla nourishes him with her milk while her tongue frees Búri from the ice nearby. Borr's sons kill him for it, and build the world from what is left: his blood is the sea, his flesh the land, his bones the mountains, his skull the sky.

audhumbla.summary: Formed from the same melting rime as Ymir, and she feeds him.
audhumbla.description: Auðumla comes out of the melting rime beside Ymir and feeds him from four rivers of milk. She herself lives on salt, licking the ice-blocks of the Void — and over three days her tongue frees a man from the ice: hair the first day, a head the second, and on the third Búri, whole. Nothing in the sources explains where she came from before that, only what she does with what little there is to eat.

buri.summary: Licked out of a block of salty rime by a cow, three days running, and the line of the gods begins with him.
buri.description: Búri comes from nowhere and nothing: Auðumla, the cow that nourishes Ymir, licks the salt-rimed ice for three days, and on the third a man stands there. He is fair and mighty, and the text gives him no parents and no story beyond that. He fathers Borr, and through Borr the whole line of the Æsir descends from a face that appeared in ice.

borr.epithet: Father of Óðinn, Vili and Vé
borr.summary: Búri's son, and the husband of a giant's daughter — the other half of Óðinn's blood.
borr.description: Borr is Búri's son, and takes Bestla, daughter of the giant Bǫlþorn, to wife. Their three sons are Óðinn, Vili and Vé. Between them, Borr and Bestla put a giant's blood and an ice-born stranger's blood into the same children — the two halves of the family that spend the whole cycle at war are already married to each other one generation up.

vili.summary: One of the three sons of Borr who make the world, and one of the three who kill Ymir to do it.
vili.description: Vili is Óðinn's brother, one of the three sons of Borr and Bestla. With Óðinn and Vé he kills Ymir and shapes earth, sea and sky from the giant's body — the same three names Loki later throws at Frigg as her lovers, in the one other place the sources name him at all.

ve.summary: The third son of Borr, present at the making of the world and rarely named again.
ve.description: Vé is Óðinn's brother, the youngest of Borr and Bestla's three sons. He stands beside Óðinn and Vili at Ymir's death and the shaping of the world that follows it, and beyond that single episode the sources have almost nothing to say about him — a name that appears at the beginning of everything and then goes quiet.

idunn.summary: Bragi's wife, and the reason the gods do not grow old.
idunn.description: Iðunn keeps, in a chest of ash-wood, the apples the gods must taste whenever age comes on them, and tasting them they are young again — a duty the whole company depends on without ever quite saying so out loud. She is Bragi's wife. The one time she and her apples go missing, Hárr calls it 'near being desperate' and puts off telling the story for later; it very nearly went badly for everyone.

bragi.summary: Renowned for eloquence beyond any other, and the reason poetry itself is called by his name.
bragi.description: Bragi is famed for wisdom and above all for fluency of speech; he knows more of skaldcraft than anyone, and skaldic art itself takes its name — bragr — from him. He is Iðunn's husband. At the feast in Lokasenna he tries to bar Loki from the hall, and it does him no good: Loki taunts him with cowardice in front of everyone, and Bragi's own gift, the right word, seems to be exactly what deserts him.

nanna.summary: Baldr's wife, and her heart breaks on his funeral ship before it is even lit.
nanna.description: Nanna is Baldr's wife. When his body is carried out to the pyre-ship Hringhorni, the sight of it breaks her heart on the spot, and she is burned beside him. Even from Hel she keeps up the forms of the living: she sends Frigg a linen smock and Fulla a gold ring, and Hermóðr carries them home along with the news that there is still a chance her husband might return.

skadi.summary: Took up arms to avenge her father, and left with a husband chosen by his feet alone.
skadi.description: Skaði marches on Ásgarðr in helm and mail to avenge Þjazi, and the gods buy her off with a strange bargain: she may choose a husband from among them, seeing nothing but their feet. She picks the fairest pair, certain they belong to Baldr, and gets Njörðr instead. The marriage does not sit easily — he wants the shore, she wants the mountains where her father lived — but the settlement holds, and she goes back to Þrymheimr on skis, with a bow, and is called the snowshoe-goddess ever after.

thjazi.summary: Trapped Loki in eagle's shape and traded his freedom for Iðunn — then paid for it with his life.
thjazi.description: Þjazi catches Loki in the form of an eagle, glues him fast to a pole, and will not let him go until he swears to lure Iðunn out of Ásgarðr with her apples. Loki keeps the oath; Þjazi carries her off to Þrymheimr in his eagle's plumage, and the gods age visibly the moment she is gone. When Loki flies her back as a nut in Freyja's hawk-dress, Þjazi gives chase in the same shape and is burned and killed at the gate of Ásgarðr. His daughter is Skaði.

utgarda-loki.summary: Beat Þórr at every contest by cheating with the shape of the world itself.
utgarda-loki.description: Útgarða-Loki receives Þórr and his companions as Skrýmir first, binding their provisions with an iron knot no one can undo, then as the king of a giant's hall where the visitors are set impossible tasks in disguise: Loki loses an eating race to wildfire, Þjálfi loses a footrace to thought, and Þórr himself only half-empties the sea, barely lifts the Midgard Serpent disguised as a cat, and is brought to one knee by old age wearing a woman's shape. Once his guests are safely outside the gate, he explains every trick — and the castle vanishes before Þórr can swing the hammer at him.

gerd.summary: So bright that sky and sea lit up when she raised her arms, and Freyr gave up his sword to win her.
gerd.description: Gerðr is the daughter of the giant Gymir and Aurboða, and fairest of all women. Freyr sees her from Hliðskjálf and falls into a grief so total he will not eat, sleep, or speak. He sends Skírnir to woo her on his behalf, paying for it with the one sword that fights on its own — the same sword whose absence leaves him weaponless against Surtr at Ragnarǫk. Gerðr agrees to the marriage nine nights later, at Barrey.

hymir.summary: Rows out with Þórr and hooks the Midgard Serpent — and is named, in one poem only, as Týr's father.
hymir.description: Hymir keeps house at the edge of the world with a cauldron large enough for all the gods' brewing, and Þórr goes to fetch it disguised as a boy. Together they row out to sea, where Þórr baits a hook with an ox's head and very nearly lands Jǫrmungandr before Hymir cuts the line in fright. Hymiskviða calls him Týr's father outright — 'a kettle my father fierce doth own' — while Skáldskaparmál names Týr Óðinn's son instead. Neither text budges, so the graph keeps both.

thrym.summary: Stole Þórr's hammer and asked for Freyja as ransom — and got Mjǫllnir back in his lap instead.
thrym.description: Þrymr steals Mjǫllnir and buries it eight leagues down, and will trade it for nothing but Freyja as his bride. Freyja refuses outright, so Þórr goes to the wedding himself, veiled and dressed as the bride, with Loki beside him as a handmaid. When the hammer is carried in to hallow the marriage, as custom asks, Þórr's heart laughs: he kills Þrymr first, then the whole hall of giants.

fenrir.summary: Raised by the gods who feared him, bound by a ribbon, and he swallows Óðinn.
fenrir.description: Fenrir is Loki and Angrboða's eldest, and the Æsir brought him up at home in Ásgarðr because the alternative was leaving him in Jǫtunheimr. He broke the fetter Læðingr and then the fetter Drómi, and the third, Gleipnir, was made by dwarves out of six impossible things and held. He agreed to it only against a pledge, and Týr's hand was the pledge, and Týr lost it. At Ragnarǫk he comes loose, swallows Óðinn, and is killed by Óðinn's son Víðarr. His own brood are the wolves that hunt the sun and moon.

jormungandr.summary: Thrown into the sea as a child, it grew until it bit its own tail.
jormungandr.description: Jǫrmungandr is the second of Loki's children by Angrboða. Óðinn threw it into the deep sea, and it grew there until it lies in the middle of the ocean encircling all the land, biting its own tail — a containment measure that became the shape of the world. Þórr fishes for it once and fails to land it. At Ragnarǫk it comes ashore, and it and Þórr kill each other: he strikes it down, walks nine paces, and falls in its venom.

hel.summary: Cast into Niflheimr as a child and given rule over the dead.
hel.description: Hel is the third of Loki's children by Angrboða. Óðinn cast her into Niflheimr and gave her authority over nine worlds, to apportion lodging to everyone sent to her — those who die of sickness or old age, rather than in battle. Snorri names her furniture: her hall Sleet-Cold, her dish Hunger, her knife Famine, her threshold Pit of Stumbling. When Baldr dies he goes to her, and she is the one who names the price of his return. At the end, her people sail.

garm.summary: Bound before the cave, howling; he and Týr kill each other.
garm.description: Garmr is bound before Gnipahellir, and Vǫluspá returns to him as a refrain — Garm howls loud, the fetters will burst, the wolf runs free. Snorri calls him the greatest of monsters and gives him to Týr at Ragnarǫk, where each becomes the other's slayer. Whether Garmr and Fenrir are two hounds or one is an old argument; the sources never resolve it, and this graph keeps them apart because that is how the sources leave them.

skoll.epithet: The wolf at the sun's heels
skoll.summary: He runs behind the sun, and one day he catches her.
skoll.description: Skǫll is the wolf that follows the sun. Snorri says she fears him and he shall take her, which he does at the beginning of the end. Grímnismál puts him at Ironwood. His parentage is a knot: Vǫluspá says an old giantess in Ironwood bore the brood of Fenrir, and Snorri says an old witch there bore many giant sons in wolf shape — the two accounts fit together only if the wolves are Fenrir's, and neither text quite says so.

hati.summary: He runs ahead of the sun, hunting the moon.
hati.description: Hati leaps before the sun rather than behind her, because what he is after is the moon. Grímnismál calls him the son of Hróðvitnir, and Snorri gives him the patronymic Hróðvitnisson; Hróðvitnir is generally taken as a byname for Fenrir, which would make Hati the wolf's son and Skǫll's brother, but no surviving text states the identification outright. He is recorded here as Fenrir's child with the certainty set to implied, which is the honest reading.

urd.summary: Her well waters Yggdrasill, and her name means what has already happened.
urd.description: Urðr is the first-named of the three maidens who come from the hall by the well under Yggdrasill's third root, and that well is called by her name — the gods hold their tribunal there every day, riding out over Bifrǫst to reach it. She, Verðandi and Skuld score the wood and set the fates of the sons of men: some are given a long life and some a short one, and the text is blunt about why — good norns of honorable race appoint a good life, and evil norns govern the rest.

verdandi.summary: One of three maidens under Yggdrasill who set the fates of men.
verdandi.description: Verðandi comes from the hall at Urðr's well with Urðr and Skuld, and together they score fate onto wood and allot the length of every human life. Vǫluspá names all three in one breath and says no more about her individually — of the sources' many norns, she is one of the three who matter most, and the corpus never separates her from her sisters long enough to give her a story of her own.

skuld.summary: Sets fates under Yggdrasill, and elsewhere rides to choose the slain.
skuld.description: Skuld is the third of the maidens who come from the hall at Urðr's well to score wood and set the length of men's lives. Snorri names a norn called Skuld again later, among the Valkyrs who ride to every battle and decide its outcome — whether that is the same figure worn two ways or two separate beings sharing a name, the text does not say, and this graph is not the one to decide it.

mimir.summary: Wisdom is stored in his well, and he drinks from it with Gjallarhorn.
mimir.description: Mímir keeps the well under the root of Yggdrasill that turns toward the rime-giants, where wisdom and understanding are stored. He is full of ancient lore because he drinks from the well, and Snorri says he drinks from it with Gjallarhorn — which is a problem, because six chapters later Gjallarhorn is Heimdallr's trumpet, the one that wakes the gods. Snorri contradicts himself inside a single work, and this project records both readings rather than choosing. Óðinn gave an eye for a drink from the well, and rides back to consult Mímir when the end begins.

asgard.summary: Built in the middle of the world, and it is where the wolf grew up.
asgard.description: Ásgarðr is the city the sons of Borr made for themselves in the middle of the world, where the gods and their kindred dwell. One of Yggdrasill's three roots reaches it. Heimdallr guards its bridge and Þórr defends it, and it is where the Æsir chose to raise Fenrir rather than leave him in Jǫtunheimr — a decision that put the instrument of Óðinn's death inside his own walls for the length of its childhood.

midgard.summary: The world of people, ringed by a serpent.
midgard.description: Miðgarðr is the world given to mankind, made by the sons of Borr and defended by Þórr. It is encircled by Jǫrmungandr, which lies in the ocean around all the land with its tail in its mouth — so the boundary of the human world is one of Loki's children. At the end, Surtr flings fire over it and burns it, and the sun turns black and the earth sinks into the sea.

jotunheim.summary: Where Angrboða raised three children the gods came to collect.
jotunheim.description: Jǫtunheimr is the giants' country, and one of Yggdrasill's roots stands among the rime-giants there. Angrboða was living in it when she and Loki had Fenrir, Jǫrmungandr and Hel, and the gods learned that the kindred was being nourished there and went to take them away. Much of the cycle is the Æsir travelling into Jǫtunheimr to break something, and being related to what they break.

niflheim.summary: Older than the earth, and Hel rules the dead there.
niflheim.description: Niflheimr was made many ages before the earth was shaped. The well Hvergelmir lies at its centre, and eleven rivers spring from it, and Yggdrasill's third root stands over it with Níðhǫggr gnawing from below. Óðinn cast Hel into it and gave her power over nine worlds, so the oldest of the cold places became the administration of the dead. Baldr goes there.

muspelheim.summary: The first world of all, light and hot and impassable, with Surtr on the border.
muspelheim.description: Múspell is the first world to exist, in the southern region: light, hot, glowing and burning, and impassable to anyone who does not hold land there. Surtr stands at its edge with a flaming sword to keep others out — a guard posted before there was anything to guard against. Its people ride out at Ragnarǫk in a company by themselves, and Snorri notes that they are very bright.

yggdrasil.summary: Three roots, three worlds, and it shakes when the end starts.
yggdrasil.description: Yggdrasill is the greatest and best of trees, its limbs spread over all the world and standing above heaven. Three roots hold it up: one among the Æsir, one among the rime-giants where the Yawning Void was, and one over Niflheimr, where Níðhǫggr gnaws it from beneath. Mímir's well is under the second. The gods give judgment at it every day. When Fenrir comes loose the Ash trembles, and nothing in heaven or earth is without fear.

mjolnir.summary: The rime-giants know it when it goes up.
mjolnir.description: Mjǫllnir is the first of Þórr's three things of great price, made by the dwarf Sindri while Loki, in the shape of a fly, tried to spoil the work. Snorri says the rime-giants and the hill-giants know it when it is raised, having lost fathers and kinsmen to it. Þórr also has a girdle that doubles his strength and iron gloves he cannot use the hammer-shaft without. After Ragnarǫk it passes to his sons Móði and Magni.

gungnir.summary: Made by Ívaldi's sons; the thrust never stops.
gungnir.description: Gungnir was made by the dwarves called Ívaldi's Sons, in the same sitting that produced Sif's golden hair and the ship Skíðblaðnir, after Loki had cut Sif's hair off and needed to make it good. Loki handed it to Óðinn himself. Its virtue is that the thrust never stops. Óðinn rides out to Ragnarǫk carrying it, in a gold helmet and a fair mail-coat, and it does not save him.

gleipnir.summary: Six impossible things, and it is soft as a ribbon.
gleipnir.description: After Fenrir broke Læðingr and Drómi, Óðinn sent Skírnir down to the Black Elves for something better. The dwarves made Gleipnir out of six things: the noise a cat makes walking, a woman's beard, the roots of a rock, the sinews of a bear, the breath of a fish, and the spittle of a bird. It looks like a silk ribbon. Fenrir would not take it without a pledge, and the pledge was Týr's hand, and the gods had no intention of letting him go.

gjallarhorn.summary: Its blast is heard in all worlds. Whose it is depends on the chapter.
gjallarhorn.description: Gjallarhorn belongs to Heimdallr, and its blast is heard throughout all the worlds; he sounds it to wake the gods when Ragnarǫk begins, and Vǫluspá has him blow it with the horn aloft. Gjallarhorn also belongs to Mímir, who drinks from the well of wisdom with it. Both statements are Snorri's, twelve chapters apart in the same book, and there is no reconciling them. The graph records both owners and lets you see the disagreement instead of hiding it.

draupnir.summary: Drops eight more rings of its own weight every ninth night.
draupnir.description: Draupnir is the ring the dwarf Sindri makes for Brokkr to carry to Ásgarðr, and its virtue is that eight rings of equal weight fall from it every ninth night. Óðinn wins the judgment that names it the second-best of the three gifts, after Mjǫllnir, and lays it on Baldr's pyre — a debt he collects on when Baldr sends the ring back from Hel with Hermóðr, a gesture that costs him nothing and gives Óðinn nothing back but the fact of it.

skidbladnir.summary: Big enough for every god in arms, and folds small enough for a pocket.
skidbladnir.description: Skíðblaðnir is made by the dwarves called Ívaldi's Sons, in the same commission that produced Sif's golden hair and the spear Gungnir. It is built with such skill that it always has a fair wind the moment its sail is raised, wherever it is bound, and it can carry all the Æsir under arms — yet when there is no use for it at sea, it folds up like a cloth and fits in a pouch. Loki gives it to Freyr.

brisingamen.summary: Hers alone — and put on Þórr only once, to make a wedding disguise convincing.
brisingamen.description: Brísingamen belongs to Freyja, and Snorri names it among her possessions without saying who made it or how she came by it. When the gods dress Þórr as the bride to win back Mjǫllnir from Þrymr, the necklace goes around his neck along with the rest of the disguise — the one time in the sources it leaves her, and only because a hammer was worth more.

mare.summary: Loki draws Svaðilfari into the woods in this shape and later bears the eight-legged foal.
mare.description: A mare runs out of the woods and draws the stallion Svaðilfari away from the builder's work, costing him the bargain he had nearly won from the gods. The text never says outright that the mare is Loki. It says instead that Loki had dealings with Svaðilfari and later gave birth to Sleipnir, which makes the identity an inference strong enough to record and honest enough to mark implied.

salmon.summary: He takes this shape at Fránangr-Falls, invents the net, and is caught by Þórr.
salmon.description: Loki hides at Fránangr-Falls in the likeness of a salmon while he works out how the gods might catch him. In doing so he invents the first fishing net and leaves its pattern in the ashes when they arrive. The gods remake it, and after he leaps the net once, Þórr catches him by the tail — the reason Snorri gives for the salmon's tapering back.

thokk.epithet: The giantess who would not weep
thokk.summary: The one refusal that keeps Baldr in Hel — and the text says people took her for Loki.
thokk.description: Þǫkk sits in a cave when the messengers ask every living and dead thing to weep Baldr out of Hel. She alone refuses, so Hel's condition fails and Baldr remains among the dead. Snorri closes the episode by saying that people believed the giantess was Loki Laufeyjarson. The identification is reported rather than asserted by the narrator, so the graph keeps it visible as implied.

woman.epithet: The shape that found Baldr's weakness
woman.summary: Loki enters Fensalir in this likeness and asks Frigg what escaped her oaths.
woman.description: Loki makes himself into the likeness of a woman and goes to Frigg at Fensalir. By asking whether every thing has sworn not to harm Baldr, he learns that mistletoe alone was thought too young to bind with an oath. He leaves in the same disguise, pulls up the shoot, and puts the one dangerous thing in the hands of Baldr's blind brother.

wolf.summary: The Æsir turn Loki's son into a wolf, and he tears apart his brother Narfi.
wolf.description: This wolf is not a separate beast and not a shape Váli chooses. When the gods seize Loki, they change his son Váli into a wolf and make one brother tear the other apart. They use Narfi's entrails to bind Loki, and the bonds turn to iron. The form records a transformation inflicted as punishment, not a display of Váli's own cunning.

vali-lokason.summary: Changed into a wolf by the Æsir and made to tear apart his brother Narfi.
vali-lokason.description: Váli Lokason appears in Snorri's account of Loki's binding as one of two sons taken by the Æsir. They change Váli into the form of a wolf, and in that form he tears Narfi apart before the gods use Narfi's entrails as Loki's bonds. His place in Loki's household belongs to a variant thread in the sources, and the transformation is something done to him, not an act he undertakes himself.

hoenir.summary: Given to the Vanir for Njǫrðr, he survives the fire and takes up prophecy afterward.
hoenir.description: Hœnir is one of the Æsir whom the Vanir take as a hostage in exchange for Njǫrðr, making him part of the peace between the two divine families. Vǫluspá places him much earlier beside Óðinn and Lóðurr at the creation of humankind, where he gives sense to Askr and Embla, and much later among the few gods left after Ragnarǫk, taking up the prophetic wand in the renewed world. The hostage crosses both settlements: the peace after the first war and the life after the last.

skirnir.summary: He carries Freyr's suit to Gerðr and returns with a wedding date, paid with the sword Freyr later needs.
skirnir.description: Skírnir is Freyr's servant and messenger. Óðinn sends him to the dwarves for Gleipnir, and Njǫrðr sends him to learn why Freyr has stopped eating, sleeping and speaking. Freyr's answer becomes an errand: woo Gerðr on his behalf. Skírnir asks for the horse that can cross flame and the sword that fights by itself, wins Gerðr's promise, and brings back a date nine nights away. The mission succeeds; its price leaves Freyr without that sword when Surtr comes.

vafthrudnir.epithet: The giant of the wisdom wager
vafthrudnir.summary: He stakes his head against a disguised Óðinn and answers everything except what only Óðinn can know.
vafthrudnir.description: Vafþrúðnir is the giant whose wisdom Frigg says no other giant can equal. Óðinn enters his hall under the name Gagnráðr, and the two test one another with questions about the first world, the nine worlds and the one that follows Ragnarǫk, wagering their heads on the result. Vafþrúðnir answers until Óðinn asks what he whispered into Baldr's ear on the pyre. Only Óðinn can know. The giant recognizes him, admits that Óðinn is wiser, and the poem ends with the wager still hanging over that admission.
